claim: Immobilised FN but not soluble FN promotes sEV secretion by VSMCs.
source: Plating VSMCs on immobilised FN increased the release of CD63+/CD81+sEVs 3.5±0.6 fold whilst addition of soluble FN had no effect on EV secretion as detected by CD63-bead capture assay (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CD63-bead capture assay shown in Figure 1A

claim: Fibrillar collagen I but not non-fibrillar laminin stimulates secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs by VSMCs to the same extent as FN.
source: Fibrillar collagen I but not a non-fibrillar laminin also stimulated secretion of CD63+/CD81 + sEVs by VSMCs to the same extent as FN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: VSMCs plated on 3D matrix acquire an elongated shape typical for mesenchymal cells in a 3D environment.
source: VSMCs acquired an elongated shape (Figure 1B and C), which is typical for mesenchymal cells in a 3D environment (Beacham et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B and C and cited reference Beacham et al., 2007

claim: 3D matrices increase secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs compared to VSMCs plated onto non-coated plastic.
source: VSMCs acquired an elongated shape (Figure 1B and C), which is typical for mesenchymal cells in a 3D environment (Beacham et al., 2007) and increased secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs compared to VSMCs plated onto the non-coated plastic (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: FN matrix does not affect the size distribution of sEVs secreted by VSMCs.
source: We observed no changes in the size distribution of sEVs secreted by VSMCs plated either on plastic or FN matrix as detected using Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis (NTA; Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by NTA data shown in Figure 1E

claim: sEVs isolated from VSMCs plated on plastic or FN matrix contain similar levels of FN, CD63, and Syntenin-1 and lack α-actinin-4.
source: To further characterise the EV populations released, western blotting confirmed that sEVs isolated in both conditions were loaded with similar levels of FN and the sEV-specific markers CD63 and Syntenin-1 and lacked the EV-specific marker, α-actinin-4 (Figure 1F; Kowal et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1F and cited reference Kowal et al., 2016

claim: CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion in response to collagen and FN is regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3.
source: In addition, treatment of the cells plated onto the matrix with sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor (3-O-Methyl-Sphingomyelin, 3-OMS) revealed that CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion in response to collagen and FN was regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data using 3-OMS inhibitor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 regulates sEV generation in multivesicular bodies.
source: In addition, treatment of the cells plated onto the matrix with sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor (3-O-Methyl-Sphingomyelin, 3-OMS) revealed that CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion in response to collagen and FN was regulated by sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) which regulates sEV generation in multivesicular bodies (Trajkovic et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Trajkovic et al., 2008

claim: FN triggers secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs with a late endosomal origin.
source: Hence, FN triggers secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs, most likely with a late endosomal origin.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing regulation by SMPD3 and presence of late endosomal markers

claim: Activation of β1 integrin using 12G10 antibody enhances the effect of FN on sEV secretion.
source: Activation of β1 integrin using 12G10 antibody in VSMCs enhanced the effect of FN on sEV secretion (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using 12G10 antibody shown in Figure 1G

claim: Inhibition of β1 integrin using 4B4 antibody blocks CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion by VSMCs plated on FN.
source: Inhibition of β1 integrin using the 4B4 antibody blocked CD63+/CD81+ sEV secretion by VSMCs plated on FN (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using 4B4 antibody shown in Figure 1G

claim: Blocking FAK and Src pathways with small inhibitors reduces sEV secretion by cells plated on FN but not on plastic.
source: Blocking these pathways with small inhibitors (FAM14 and PP2, respectively) reduced sEV secretion by cells plated on FN but not on plastic (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using FAM14 and PP2 inhibitors shown in Figure 1H and I

claim: FN matrices stimulate secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs via the β1 integrin signalling pathway.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that FN matrices stimulate secretion of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs via the β1 integrin signalling pathway.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing effects of β1 integrin activation/inhibition and downstream signaling

claim: CK666 reduces sEV secretion both in VSMCs plated on plastic and FN matrix.
source: CK666 reduced sEV secretion both in VSMCs plated on plastic and FN matrix, while inhibition of formins using SMIFH2 was only effective on the FN matrix (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CK666 inhibitor shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Inhibition of formins using SMIFH2 is only effective on the FN matrix.
source: CK666 reduced sEV secretion both in VSMCs plated on plastic and FN matrix, while inhibition of formins using SMIFH2 was only effective on the FN matrix (Figure 2A and B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data using SMIFH2 inhibitor shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: Formins may be involved in FN-dependent sEV secretion.
source: CK666 reduced sEV secretion both in VSMCs plated on plastic and FN matrix, while inhibition of formins using SMIFH2 was only effective on the FN matrix (Figure 2A and B), indicating that formins may be involved in FN-dependent sEV secretion.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effect of SMIFH2 on FN matrix

claim: Transported MVBs are attached to F-actin tails in VSMCs.
source: Analysis of the intracellular distribution of F-actin and CD63-positive endosomes in VSMCs showed CD63-MVB propulsion by the F-actin tail in live cells (Figure 2C and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Video 2

claim: Cortactin/F-actin spots colocalise with CD63+ endosomes in VSMCs.
source: Although these were rare events, possibly due to the short observational time in a single microscopic plane (Figure 2C), we observed numerous F-actin spots in fixed VSMCs that were positive both for F-actin and cortactin, indicating that these are branched-actin tails (Figure 2D). Moreover, cortactin/F-actin spots colocalised with CD63+ endosomes
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Addition of SMPD3 inhibitor 3-OMS induces the appearance of enlarged doughnut-like cortactin/F-actin/CD63 complexes resembling invadopodia-like structures.
source: Moreover, cortactin/F-actin spots colocalised with CD63+ endosomes and addition of the SMPD3 inhibitor, 3-OMS, induced the appearance of enlarged doughnut-like cortactin/F-actin/CD63 complexes resembling invadopodia-like structures similar to those observed in tumour cells (Figure 2D, arrows; Hoshino et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and cited reference Hoshino et al., 2013

claim: Approximately 50% of F-actin tails are associated with ~13% of all endosomes in VSMCs.
source: Approximately 50% of the F-actin tails were associated with ~13% of all endosomes (tM1=0.44 ± 0.23 and tM2=0.13 ± 0.06, respectively, N=3).
evidence: Supported by quantitative colocalization analysis

claim: Addition of 3-OMS enhances overlap between F-actin tails and CD63+ endosomes.
source: Addition of 3-OMS enhanced this overlap further (tM1=0.75 ± 0.18 and tM2=0.25 ± 0.09)
evidence: Supported by quantitative colocalization analysis with 3-OMS treatment

claim: Arp2/3-driven branched F-actin tails are involved in CD63+MVB intracellular transport in VSMCs.
source: Addition of 3-OMS enhanced this overlap further (tM1=0.75 ± 0.18 and tM2=0.25 ± 0.09) suggesting that Arp2/3-driven branched F-actin tails are involved in CD63 +MVB intracellular transport in VSMCs.
evidence: Inferred from colocalization data and effects of inhibitors

claim: There is no difference in total filopodia number per cell on plastic or FN matrices.
source: We observed no difference between total filopodia number per cell on plastic or FN matrices (n=18 ± 8 and n=14 ± 3, respectively)
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of filopodia

claim: Endogenous CD63+ MVBs are present along Myo10-positive filopodia in both plastic and FN conditions.
source: We observed no difference between total filopodia number per cell on plastic or FN matrices (n=18 ± 8 and n=14 ± 3, respectively); however, the presence of endogenous CD63+ MVBs along the Myo10-positive filopodia was observed in both conditions (Figure 2E, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Anterograde MVB transport toward the filopodia tip occurs in live VSMCs.
source: Importantly, we observed anterograde MVB transport toward the filopodia tip (Figure 2F and Video 3) indicative of MVB secretion.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2F and Video 3

claim: Typical 'burst'-like appearance of sEV secretion occurs at the cell-ECM interface.
source: Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRF), we observed the typical 'burst'-like appearance of sEV secretion at the cell-ECM interface in full agreement with an earlier report showing MVB recruitment to invadopodia-like structures in tumor cells (Hoshino et al., 2013; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 4).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Video 4, and cited reference Hoshino et al., 2013

claim: sEV secretion by VSMCs is regulated via Arp2/3 and formin-dependent actin cytoskeleton remodelling.
source: Taken together, these data show that sEV secretion by VSMCs is regulated via Arp2/3 and formin-dependent actin cytoskeleton remodelling.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing effects of Arp2/3 and formin inhibitors

claim: Branched actin tails can potentially contribute to MVB intracellular transport and secretion at the VSMC-ECM interface.
source: Branched actin tails can potentially contribute to MVB intracellular transport and secretion at the VSMC-ECM interface.
evidence: Speculative statement based on observed colocalization and transport

claim: CD63+MVBs can be observed in filopodia-like structures.
source: Interestingly, CD63+MVBs can be observed in filopodia-like structures, suggesting that sEV secretion can also occur spatially via cellular protrusion-like filopodia, but more studies are needed to confirm this hypothesis.
evidence: Observed in imaging data but noted as requiring further confirmation

claim: EV trapping in the ECM is a prominent feature of the blood vessel media and intima.
source: EV trapping in the ECM is a prominent feature of the blood vessel media and intima, and EVs become more abundant in the ECM with ageing and disease (Hutcheson et al., 2016; Whitehead et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by cited references Hutcheson et al., 2016 and Whitehead et al., 2023

claim: CD63+ sEVs are observed both on plastic and FN-coated plates in proximity to protrusions at the cell periphery.
source: We observed CD63 puncta in proximity to protrusions at the cell periphery (Figure 3A). These CD63+ sEVs were observed both on the plastic and FN-coated plates
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A

claim: sEVs can bind to the ECM secreted by VSMCs over 24 hr incubation.
source: These CD63+ sEVs were observed both on the plastic and FN-coated plates, suggesting that sEVs can bind to the ECM secreted by VSMCs over the 24 hr incubation.
evidence: Inferred from observation of sEVs on both surfaces

claim: CD63+ sEV trapping in native ECM is reduced when VSMCs are treated with SMPD3 siRNA.
source: In agreement with our previous data, we also observed CD63+ sEV trapping in the native ECM produced by VSMCs over a 7-day period and their reduction/absence from the matrix when VSMCs were treated with SMPD3 siRNA (Figure 3B; Whitehead et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B and cited reference Whitehead et al., 2023

claim: EVs are both loosely bound and strongly trapped within the ECM.
source: The total particle count showed that EVs are both loosely bound and strongly trapped within the ECM.
evidence: Supported by sequential extraction and ExoView analysis

claim: There is close similarity between conditioned media and 0.5 M NaCl fraction with high abundance of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs.
source: sEV tetraspanin profiling showed differences between these 3 EV populations. While there was close similarity between the conditioned media and the 0.5 M NaCl fraction with high abundance of CD63+/CD81+ sEVs as well as CD63+/CD81+/CD9+ in both fractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ExoView analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The GuHCl fraction is particularly enriched with CD63+ and CD63+/CD81+ sEVs with very low abundance of CD9+ EVs.
source: In contrast, the GuHCl fraction was particularly enriched with CD63+ and CD63+/CD81+ sEVs with very low abundance of CD9+ EVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ExoView analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Prothrombin binds to the sEV surface both in the media and MVB lumen and is recycled in sEVs.
source: We previously found that the serum protein prothrombin binds to the sEV surface both in the media and MVB lumen, showing it is recycled in sEVs and catalyses thrombogenesis being on the sEV surface (Kapustin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Kapustin et al., 2017

claim: FN is endocytosed and delivered to early and late endosomes together with fetuin A in serum-deprived VSMCs.
source: We treated serum-deprived primary human aortic VSMCs with FN-Alexa568 and found that it was endocytosed and subsequently delivered to early and late endosomes together with fetuin A, another abundant serum protein that is a recycled sEV cargo and elevated in plaques (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: FN colocalises with CD63+MVBs in VSMCs.
source: CD63 visualisation with a different fluorophore (Alexa488) confirmed FN colocalisation with CD63+MVBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Colocalisation of CD63 and serum-derived FN is reduced in non-serum deprived cells likely due to competitive bulk protein uptake.
source: Next, we stained non-serum deprived VMC cultured in normal growth media supplemented with serum (M199 supplemented with 2.5% sEV-free FBS) with an anti-FN antibody and observed colocalisation of CD63 and serum-derived FN. Co-localisation was reduced, likely due to competitive bulk protein uptake by non-deprived cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F with inference about mechanism

claim: FN intracellular spots and colocalisation with CD63 disappear in confluent VSMCs.
source: Notably, when we compared FN distribution in sparsely growing VSMCs versus confluent cells, we found that FN intracellular spots, as well as colocalisation with CD63, completely disappeared in the confluent state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: Confluent VSMCs show nearly complete loss of CD63+/CD81+sEV secretion.
source: This correlated with nearly complete loss of CD63+/CD81+sEV secretion by the confluent cells, indicating that confluence abrogates intracellular FN trafficking as well as sEV secretion by VSMCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by CD63-bead assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H

claim: Confluence abrogates intracellular FN trafficking and sEV secretion by VSMCs.
source: This correlated with nearly complete loss of CD63+/CD81+sEV secretion by the confluent cells, indicating that confluence abrogates intracellular FN trafficking as well as sEV secretion by VSMCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Inferred from correlation between FN trafficking and sEV secretion at different cell densities

claim: FN can be co-purified with sEVs from VSMC conditioned media.
source: Finally, FN could be co-purified with sEVs from VSMC conditioned media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I

claim: FN is detected on the surface of sEVs by flow cytometry.
source: Finally, FN could be co-purified with sEVs from VSMC conditioned media (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I) and detected on the surface of sEVs by flow cytometry confirming its loading and secretion via sEVs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Addition of sEVs to cell media results in fast uptake by VSMCs and delivery to the nuclear periphery.
source: Super-resolution microscopy (iSIM) revealed that the addition of sEVs to the cell media resulted in fast uptake by VSMCs and delivery to the nuclear periphery (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1J

claim: Purified sEVs added to FN-coated plates are not internalised even 24 hr after cell addition.
source: In contrast, purified sEVs added to FN-coated plates resulting in their even distribution across the ECM were not internalised even 24 hr after cell addition with no perinuclear localisation of ECM-associated sEVs observed (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1K

claim: Unbiased proteomics analysis revealed 213 plaque-specific and 111 intact arterial-specific proteins.
source: Unbiased proteomics analysis confirmed considerable differences between these 2 sample groups, revealing 213 plaque-specific and 111 intact arterial-specific proteins (Figure 4A and B, Supplementary file 1; Supplementary file 2; Supplementary file 3; Supplementary file 4; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 4A and B and supplementary files

claim: Differential expression analysis identified 46 proteins significantly overexpressed in plaques and 13 proteins significantly upregulated in intact arterial segments.
source: Differential expression analysis identified 46 proteins significantly overexpressed (fold change ≥2 and FDR-adjusted p-value ≤0.05) in plaques and 13 proteins significantly upregulated in the intact arterial segments (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 3

claim: Fetuin-A is accumulated in atherosclerotic regions with a 2.7-fold increase.
source: Comparison of the differentially expressed proteins also revealed an accumulation in atherosclerotic regions of fetuin-A (Alpha-2-HS-glycoprotein, P02765, 2.7-fold increase, p=0.003869659), an abundant sEV cargo protein which is recycled by VSMCs (Kapustin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data and cited reference Kapustin et al., 2015

claim: Apolipoprotein B-100 level is significantly elevated in atherosclerotic plaque with a 2.8-fold increase.
source: Likewise, the level of another sEV cargo, Apolipoprotein B-100 (P04114) was also significantly elevated (2.8-fold increase, p=0.000124446) in atherosclerotic plaque (Supplementary file 2; Kapustin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 2 and cited reference Kapustin et al., 2015

claim: Coronin 1C, a negative regulator of sEV secretion, is downregulated in the plaque with a 0.6-fold decrease.
source: Notably, a negative regulator of sEV secretion, Coronin 1C (Q9ULV4) was downregulated in the plaque (0.6-fold decrease, p=0.000805372, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 2

claim: Downregulation of Coronin 1C is consistent with previous studies suggesting that sEV secretion is upregulated during plaque progression.
source: Notably, a negative regulator of sEV secretion, Coronin 1C (Q9ULV4) was downregulated in the plaque (0.6-fold decrease, p=0.000805372, Supplementary file 2) consistent with previous studies that suggested that sEV secretion is upregulated during plaque progression (Hutcheson et al., 2016; Tagliatela et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references Hutcheson et al., 2016 and Tagliatela et al., 2020

claim: FN accumulates both in the neointima and the tunica media where it is significantly colocalised with the sEV marker CD81.
source: Using this clear morphological demarcation, we found that FN accumulated both in the neointima and the tunica media where it was significantly colocalised with the sEV marker, CD81 (Figure 4D, E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D, E and F

claim: CD81 and FN colocalisation is particularly prominent in cell-free, matrix-rich plaque regions.
source: Notably, CD81 and FN colocalisation was particularly prominent in cell-free, matrix-rich plaque regions (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4E and F

claim: There is a trend of higher colocalisation levels of CD81 with FN in the neointima compared to tunica media, which is not significant.
source: Interestingly, colocalisation analysis of CD81 and FN distribution showed that there was a trend of higher colocalisation levels of CD81 with FN in the neointima as compared to tunica media, which was not significant (Thresholded Mander's split colocalisation coefficient for CD81 colocalisation with FN 0.58±0.21 and 0.49±0.14, respectively, N=13, p=0.052, paired T test).
evidence: Supported by quantitative colocalization analysis

claim: The majority of CD31 colocalises with CD81 in atherosclerotic plaques.
source: In agreement with a previous study, we found that the majority of CD31 colocalises with CD81 (Thresholded Mander's split colocalisation coefficient 0.54±0.11, N=6) indicating that endothelial cells express CD81 (Figure 4G; Rohlena et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 4G and cited reference Rohlena et al., 2009

claim: Only a minor fraction of total CD81 colocalises with CD31, confirming that the majority of CD81 in the neointima originates from VSMCs.
source: However, only a minor fraction of total CD81 colocalised with CD31 (Thresholded Mander's split colocalisation coefficient 0.24±0.06, N=6) confirming that the majority of CD81 in the neointima is originating from the most abundant VSMCs.
evidence: Supported by quantitative colocalization analysis with inference about cell origin

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed FN accumulation in the plaque region.
source: Finally, western blot analysis confirmed FN accumulation in the plaque region (Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: FN expression could not be detected in plaques or intact vessels by RT-PCR, but was abundant in the liver.
source: To understand the origin of plaque FN, we performed RT-PCR. FN expression could neither be detected in plaques nor in intact vessels, although it was abundant in the liver (data not shown)
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data (not shown)

claim: The circulation is a key source of FN in atherosclerotic plaques.
source: To understand the origin of plaque FN, we performed RT-PCR. FN expression could neither be detected in plaques nor in intact vessels, although it was abundant in the liver (data not shown), suggesting that the circulation is a key source of FN in atherosclerotic plaques.
evidence: Inferred from RT-PCR data showing liver expression but not vessel expression

claim: FN coating promotes VSMC velocity in a 2D single-cell migration model.
source: We found that FN coating promoted VSMC velocity and inhibition of bulk sEV secretion with 3-OMS reduced VSMC speed in a 2D single-cell migration model (Figure 5A and B)
evidence: Supported by 2D migration assay data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: Inhibition of bulk sEV secretion with 3-OMS reduces VSMC speed in a 2D single-cell migration model.
source: We found that FN coating promoted VSMC velocity and inhibition of bulk sEV secretion with 3-OMS reduced VSMC speed in a 2D single-cell migration model (Figure 5A and B) in agreement with previous studies using tumour cells (Sung et al., 2015; Sung and Weaver, 2017).
evidence: Supported by 2D migration assay data shown in Figure 5A and B and cited references Sung et al., 2015 and Sung and Weaver, 2017

claim: Addition of sEVs to the ECM has no effect on VSMC speed at baseline but rescues cell speed and distance in the presence of 3-OMS.
source: However, the addition of sEVs to the ECM had no effect on VSMC speed at baseline but rescued cell speed and distance in the presence of the sEV secretion inhibitor, 3-OMS, suggesting the EVs are not primarily regulating cell speed (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by 2D migration assay data shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: sEVs are not primarily regulating cell speed.
source: However, the addition of sEVs to the ECM had no effect on VSMC speed at baseline but rescued cell speed and distance in the presence of the sEV secretion inhibitor, 3-OMS, suggesting the EVs are not primarily regulating cell speed (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that sEVs have no effect at baseline

claim: Addition of sEVs has no effect on cell speed, accumulated distance, or straightness in 3D invasion assay.
source: The addition of sEVs had no effect on cell speed, accumulated distance, or straightness (Figure 5D, E and F).
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 5D, E and F

claim: VSMCs invading in the presence of embedded sEVs migrate more aligned to the FBS gradient compared to cells plated in the absence of sEVs.
source: However, VSMCs invading in the presence of embedded sEVs migrated more aligned to the FBS gradient compared to cells plated in the absence of sEVs.
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data

claim: Larger EVs pelleted at 10,000x g have no effect on VSMC invasion directionality.
source: To test whether this was a feature of all EV populations, we also performed the experiment in the presence of larger EVs pelleted at the 10,000x g centrifugation step and observed no effect suggesting this mechanism was specific to sEVs (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: ECM-associated sEVs have modest influence on VSMC speed but influence VSMC invasion directionality.
source: Hence, ECM-associated sEVs have modest influence on VSMC speed but influence VSMC invasion directionality.
evidence: Inferred from multiple migration and invasion assay results

claim: A marked reduction of VSMC adhesion to FN occurs in the presence of sEVs.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a marked reduction of VSMC adhesion to FN in the presence of sEVs (Figure 6A), suggesting that ECM-associated sEV can impair VSMC adhesion.
evidence: Supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: ECM-associated sEVs can impair VSMC adhesion.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a marked reduction of VSMC adhesion to FN in the presence of sEVs (Figure 6A), suggesting that ECM-associated sEV can impair VSMC adhesion.
evidence: Inferred from adhesion assay results

claim: FN alone stimulates VSMC spreading and adhesion.
source: As expected, FN alone stimulated VSMC spreading and adhesion (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by xCELLigence adhesion assay data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Addition of sEVs does not impact cellular adhesion over the first ~15 min but then adhesion is stalled.
source: Addition of sEVs did not impact cellular adhesion over the first ~15 min but then the adhesion was stalled in the presence of sEVs (Figure 6B and C), suggesting a defect in further cellular spreading.
evidence: Supported by xCELLigence adhesion assay data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: sEVs cause a defect in cellular spreading.
source: Addition of sEVs did not impact cellular adhesion over the first ~15 min but then the adhesion was stalled in the presence of sEVs (Figure 6B and C), suggesting a defect in further cellular spreading.
evidence: Inferred from the stalling of adhesion in xCELLigence assay

claim: Larger EVs pelleted at 10,000 x g have no effect on VSMC adhesion and spreading onto the FN matrix.
source: Again, to test whether this was specific for the sEV subset, we also tested the effect of larger EVs pelleted at 10,000 x g and found that these EVs had no effect on VSMC adhesion and spreading onto the FN matrix (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by xCELLigence adhesion assay data shown in Figure 6B and C

claim: Plating VSMCs onto FN increases cell size, number of FAs, and number of centripetal FAs compared to cells spreading over non-coated plastic.
source: Once again, plating VSMCs onto FN increased the cell size, number of FAs as well as the number of centripetal FAs as compared to cells spreading over non-coated plastic (Figure 6E–I).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6E–I

claim: Addition of sEVs to FN significantly reduces the number of FAs, and newly formed FAs are formed in close proximity to the cell periphery.
source: Importantly, the addition of sEVs to FN significantly reduced the number of FAs, and the newly formed FAs were formed in close proximity to the cell periphery (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and F

claim: The average FA size is similar between various conditions (plastic, FN, FN+sEVs).
source: Interestingly, the average FA size was similar between the various conditions (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 6I

claim: The FA turnover index remains the same in the presence of sEVs.
source: Interestingly, the FA turnover index remains the same in the presence of sEVs, indicating that FA stability was not altered (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by FA turnover analysis shown in Figure 6J

claim: FA stability is not altered by sEVs.
source: Interestingly, the FA turnover index remains the same in the presence of sEVs, indicating that FA stability was not altered (Figure 6J).
evidence: Inferred from FA turnover data

claim: sEVs are not influencing FA assembly or 'life-cycle' directly.
source: These data correlate well with no changes observed in FA average size across various conditions (Figure 6I) and indicate that sEVs are not influencing FA assembly or 'life-cycle' directly.
evidence: Inferred from FA size and turnover data

claim: The traction force is increased in the presence of sEVs.
source: Importantly, the traction force was increased in the presence of sEVs (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by pillar displacement analysis shown in Figure 6K

claim: ECM-associated sEVs can trigger the formation of FAs with enhanced pulling force at the cell periphery.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that ECM-associated sEVs can trigger the formation of FAs with enhanced pulling force at the cell periphery.
evidence: Inferred from FA location and traction force data

claim: 257 proteins were identified in sEVs and 168 proteins in EVs with 142 proteins common between both datasets.
source: We identified 257 proteins in sEVs and 168 proteins in EVs with 142 proteins common between both datasets (Figure 7A, Supplementary files 6-8, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 7A and supplementary files

claim: The top 5 functional enrichment clusters in sEVs are related to cell migration: ECM organisation, movement of cell or subcellular component, cell adhesion, leukocyte migration, and cell-cell adhesion.
source: Functional enrichment analysis revealed that the top 5 clusters were related to cell migration - ECM organisation, movement of cell or subcellular component, cell adhesion, leukocyte migration, and cell-cell adhesion (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by GO pathway analysis shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: The cell adhesion cluster includes collagen VI, FN, thrombospondin, EDIL3, and TGFBI.
source: The cell adhesion cluster included collagen VI (chains COL6A1, COL6A2, and COL6A3), extracellular matrix glycoproteins (FN and thrombospondin, THBS2, THBS1) as well as EGF-like repeat and discoidin I-like domain-containing protein (EDIL3) and transforming growth factor-beta-induced protein ig-h3 (TGFBI; Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 7B and supplementary files

claim: sEV proteins are predominantly involved in cell-matrix interactions and cellular adhesion.
source: Notably, these sEV proteins are predominantly involved in cell-matrix interactions and cellular adhesion.
evidence: Inferred from GO pathway analysis

claim: LGALS3BP is presented exclusively in sEVs.
source: The lectin galactoside-binding soluble 3 binding protein (LGALS3BP), which regulates cell adhesion and motility, was also presented exclusively in sEVs (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 6

claim: Collagen VI, TGFBI, EDIL, and LGALS3BP are either uniquely or highly enriched in sEVs compared to larger EVs.
source: These cell adhesion modulating proteins, including Collagen VI, TGFBI, EDIL, and LGALS3BP, were either uniquely or highly enriched in sEVs compared to larger EVs as detected by western blotting (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Collagen VI is the most abundant protein in VSMC-derived sEVs.
source: Collagen VI was the most abundant protein in VSMC-derived sEVs (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 7)
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 7

claim: Collagen VI was previously implicated in interaction with the proteoglycan NG2.
source: Collagen VI was the most abundant protein in VSMC-derived sEVs (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 7) and was previously implicated in the interaction with the proteoglycan NG2 (Tillet et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by cited reference Tillet et al., 2002

claim: Collagen VI suppresses cell spreading on FN.
source: Collagen VI was the most abundant protein in VSMC-derived sEVs (Figure 7B, Supplementary file 7) and was previously implicated in the interaction with the proteoglycan NG2 (Tillet et al., 2002) and suppression of cell spreading on FN (Nishida et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Nishida et al., 2018

claim: Both collagen VI and FN are present in sEVs extracted from 3D matrix using 0.5 M NaCl treatment.
source: To confirm the presence of collagen VI in ECM-associated sEVs, we analysed sEVs extracted from the 3D matrix using 0.5 M NaCl treatment and showed that both collagen VI and FN are present (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Alix is preferentially a luminal protein in sEVs.
source: Alix staining was bright only upon permeabilisation of sEV, indicating that it is preferentially a luminal protein (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by dot-blot data shown in Figure 7E

claim: CD63 is a surface protein in sEVs.
source: On the contrary, CD63 staining was similar in both conditions, showing that it is a surface protein (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by dot-blot data shown in Figure 7E

claim: 40% of collagen VI is located on the outside surface of sEVs with 60% in the sEV lumen.
source: Interestingly, collagen VI staining revealed that 40% of the protein is located on the outside surface with 60% in the sEV lumen (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by dot-blot quantification shown in Figure 7E

claim: Addition of anti-collagen VI antibody restores VSMC spreading on FN matrix compared to non-specific IgG treatment.
source: Addition of the anti-collagen VI antibody restored VSMC spreading on the FN matrix as compared to non-specific IgG treatment (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by xCELLigence adhesion assay data shown in Figure 7F

claim: sEVs isolated from VSMCs after collagen VI knockdown have no effect on cell speed or direction in 3D invasion model.
source: Moreover, sEVs isolated from VSMCs after collagen VI knockdown using siRNA had no effect in the 3D invasion model on cell speed (Figure 7G) or direction (Figure 7H)
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 7G and H

claim: sEVs isolated from VSMCs after collagen VI knockdown reduce cell alignment to the gradient compared to scrambled siRNA control.
source: Moreover, sEVs isolated from VSMCs after collagen VI knockdown using siRNA had no effect in the 3D invasion model on cell speed (Figure 7G) or direction (Figure 7H) but reduced cell alignment to the gradient as compared to VSMCs treated with a scrambled siRNA control (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 7I

claim: Collagen VI and TGFBI expression are significantly elevated in atherosclerotic plaques.
source: Finally, we compared the expression of collagen VI, EDIL3, and TGFBI between the plaque and control aorta tissues (Supplementary file 1). Importantly, collagen VI and TGFBI expression were significantly elevated in the plaque (Figure 7J)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7J

claim: Elevated collagen VI and TGFBI expression is consistent with increased deposition of sEVs during disease progression.
source: Importantly, collagen VI and TGFBI expression were significantly elevated in the plaque (Figure 7J), consistent with increased deposition of sEVs during disease progression.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between protein expression and sEV deposition

claim: sEVs can induce early formation of mature peripheral FAs by presenting collagen VI.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that sEVs can induce early formation of mature peripheral FAs by presenting collagen VI, thus acting to modulate cell directionality upon the invasion (Graphical Abstract).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing collagen VI effects on FA formation and cell directionality

claim: FN is a novel marker of unstable plaques.
source: Here, we show that FN, a novel marker of unstable plaques (Langley et al., 2017), enables VSMC migration and invasion by stimulating secretion of collagen VI-loaded sEVs which decorate the ECM and stimulate FA maturation.
evidence: Supported by cited reference Langley et al., 2017

claim: FN enables VSMC migration and invasion by stimulating secretion of collagen VI-loaded sEVs which decorate the ECM and stimulate FA maturation.
source: Here, we show that FN, a novel marker of unstable plaques (Langley et al., 2017), enables VSMC migration and invasion by stimulating secretion of collagen VI-loaded sEVs which decorate the ECM and stimulate FA maturation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results throughout the study

claim: EV secretion by tumour cells enhances nascent adhesion formation, facilitating tumour cell migration and invasion.
source: Notably, our data are consistent and extend previous reports showing that EV secretion by tumour cells enhances nascent adhesion formation, hence facilitating tumour cell migration and invasion (Sung et al., 2015; Sung and Weaver, 2017; Sung et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references Sung et al., 2015, Sung and Weaver, 2017, and Sung et al., 2020

claim: sEVs induce formation of FAs with enhanced pulling force at the cell periphery, favouring actomyosin-mediated contractility essential for cell body propulsion and locomotion.
source: In particular, we found that sEVs induce formation of FAs with an enhanced pulling force at the cell periphery, thus favouring actomyosin-mediated contractility which is essential for cell body propulsion and locomotion.
evidence: Inferred from FA formation and traction force data

claim: Cell directionality is guided via the integrin β1 'probe' on the tip of cellular protrusions, filopodia, and lamellipodia.
source: Cell directionality is guided via the integrin β1 'probe' on the tip of cellular protrusions, filopodia, and lamellipodia (Galbraith et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Galbraith et al., 2007

claim: Cellular protrusions are attached to the ECM via focal complexes and extended by physical force generated by branched network of actin filaments beneath the plasma membrane.
source: Cellular protrusions are attached to the ECM via focal complexes and extended by the physical force generated by the branched network of actin filaments beneath the plasma membrane (Pollard and Borisy, 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Pollard and Borisy, 2003

claim: Focal complexes either disassemble or mature into elongated centripetally located FAs.
source: Focal complexes either disassemble or mature into the elongated centripetally located FAs (Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996

claim: Mature FAs anchor the ECM to actin stress fibres and traction force generated by actomyosin-mediated contractility pulls the FAs rearward and the cell body forward.
source: In turn, these mature FAs anchor the ECM to actin stress fibres and the traction force generated by actomyosin-mediated contractility pulls the FAs rearward and the cell body forward (Sheetz et al., 1998; Ridley, 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited references Sheetz et al., 1998 and Ridley, 2001

claim: β1 integrin activation triggers sEV release followed by sEV entrapment by the ECM.
source: Here, we report that β1 integrin activation triggers sEV release followed by sEV entrapment by the ECM.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing β1 integrin effects on sEV secretion and ECM trapping

claim: FN stimulates VSMC spreading by increasing the number of FAs formed centripetally from the cell plasma membrane.
source: FN stimulated VSMC spreading by increasing the number of FAs, which were formed centripetally from the cell plasma membrane.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy data

claim: FN-associated sEVs dramatically cease VSMC spreading by inducing early formation of mature FAs at the cell periphery.
source: FN-associated sEV dramatically ceased VSMC spreading by inducing early formation of mature FAs at the cell periphery.
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy and adhesion assay data

claim: Cell spreading and adhesion are orchestrated by the Rho family of small GTPases, Cdc42, Rac1, and Rho.
source: Cell spreading and adhesion are orchestrated by the Rho family of small GTPases, Cdc42, Rac1, and Rho, with Cdc42 and Rac1 modulating filopodia and lamellipodia and focal complex formation and Rho controlling FA maturation and actomyosin-mediated contractility (Nobes and Hall, 1995; Ridley and Hall, 1992; Price et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by cited references Nobes and Hall, 1995, Ridley and Hall, 1992, and Price et al., 1998

claim: Rho is specifically degraded in cellular protrusions in fibroblasts.
source: Interestingly, in fibroblasts, Rho is specifically degraded in cellular protrusions and cellular spreading on FN is accompanied by transient Rho suppression during the fast cell spreading phase (Arthur and Burridge, 2001; Ren et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited references Arthur and Burridge, 2001, Ren et al., 1999, and Wang et al., 2003

claim: Cellular spreading on FN is accompanied by transient Rho suppression during the fast cell spreading phase.
source: Interestingly, in fibroblasts, Rho is specifically degraded in cellular protrusions and cellular spreading on FN is accompanied by transient Rho suppression during the fast cell spreading phase (Arthur and Burridge, 2001; Ren et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited references Arthur and Burridge, 2001, Ren et al., 1999, and Wang et al., 2003

claim: Rho activation leads to formation of actin stress fibres, tension increase on focal complexes and their maturation into elongated centripetally located FAs.
source: This phase is followed by Rho activation leading to formation of actin stress fibres, tension increase on the focal complexes and their maturation into elongated centripetally located FAs (Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996; Arthur and Burridge, 2001; Ren et al., 1999; Rottner et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited references Chrzanowska-Wodnicka and Burridge, 1996, Arthur and Burridge, 2001, Ren et al., 1999, and Rottner et al., 1999

claim: Excessive Rho activation leads to premature FA assembly and stress fibre formation, resulting in reduced cellular protrusions, inhibition of cellular spreading and motility on FN matrix.
source: Excessive Rho activation leads to premature FA assembly and stress fibre formation, resulting in reduced cellular protrusions, inhibition of cellular spreading and motility on the FN matrix (Arthur and Burridge, 2001; Ren et al., 1999; Roberts et al., 2003; Nobes and Hall, 1999; Cox et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited references Arthur and Burridge, 2001, Ren et al., 1999, Roberts et al., 2003, Nobes and Hall, 1999, and Cox et al., 2001

claim: Rho activity in mesenchymal cells with extensive FA networks can slow down cell migration by immobilising cells.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that Rho activity, in mesenchymal cells with extensive FA networks such as fibroblasts or VSMCs, can slow down cell migration by immobilising cells (Ridley, 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Ridley, 2001 and inference from previous statements

claim: sEV-induced FAs are spatially restricted to the cell periphery near cellular protrusions and are characterised by enhanced pulling force activity.
source: However, we found that sEVs were not influencing mature FA stability. On the contrary, sEV-induced FAs were spatially restricted to the cell periphery near cellular protrusions and were characterised by an enhanced pulling force activity.
evidence: Supported by FA turnover and traction force data

claim: Fibroblast polarisation is driven by Smurf1-dependent RhoA ubiquitinylation and localised degradation in cellular protrusions.
source: Interestingly, fibroblast polarisation is driven by Smurf1-dependent RhoA ubiquitinylation and localised degradation in cellular protrusions (Wang et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Wang et al., 2003

claim: Rho-dependent contractility is essential for cell invasion in a 3D model.
source: A recent study indicated that Rho-dependent contractility is essential for cell invasion in a 3D model and it is tempting to speculate that local Rho activity can enable VSMC invasion by stabilising FAs at the leading edge and stimulating actomyosin-mediated contractility and cell body movement (Matera et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Matera et al., 2021

claim: Rho–ROCK activity is critical for protease-independent rounded motility of tumour cells and cell types with few adhesion contacts (ameboid).
source: On the other hand, Rho–ROCK activity is critical for the protease-independent rounded motility of tumour cells and cell types with few adhesion contacts (ameboid) when Rho-dependent contractile forces generate hydrostatic pressure forming multiple membrane blebs to invade the ECM (Sahai and Marshall, 2003; Sanz-Moreno et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited references Sahai and Marshall, 2003 and Sanz-Moreno et al., 2008

claim: Extensive secretion of sEVs effectively ceases protrusion activity and VSMCs acquire a rounded morphology when 'hovering' over the FN matrix decorated with sEVs.
source: In fact, we observed that an extensive secretion of sEVs effectively ceased protrusion activity; also, VSMCs acquired a rounded morphology when 'hovering' over the FN matrix decorated with sEVs (data not shown).
evidence: Observed in experiments but data not shown

claim: Collagen VI is a nonfibrillar collagen that assembles into beaded microfilaments upon secretion and plays both structural and signalling roles.
source: Collagen VI is a nonfibrillar collagen that assembles into beaded microfilaments upon secretion and it plays both structural and signalling roles (Okada et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Okada et al., 2007

claim: Type VI collagen deposition by interstitial fibroblasts is increased in the infarcted myocardium.
source: Interestingly, type VI collagen deposition by interstitial fibroblasts is increased in the infarcted myocardium and collagen VI knockout in mice improves cardiac function, structure and remodelling after myocardial infarction via unknown pathways (Bryant et al., 2009; Luther et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references Bryant et al., 2009 and Luther et al., 2012

claim: Collagen VI knockout in mice improves cardiac function, structure and remodelling after myocardial infarction via unknown pathways.
source: Interestingly, type VI collagen deposition by interstitial fibroblasts is increased in the infarcted myocardium and collagen VI knockout in mice improves cardiac function, structure and remodelling after myocardial infarction via unknown pathways (Bryant et al., 2009; Luther et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references Bryant et al., 2009 and Luther et al., 2012

claim: In healthy vasculature, collagen VI is detected in the endothelial basement membrane in the intima and forms fibrillar structures between smooth muscle cells in the media.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis showed that in the healthy vasculature, collagen VI is detected in the endothelial basement membrane in the intima and it also forms fibrillar structures between smooth muscle cells in the media.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical analysis

claim: In fibrous plaque, collagen VI is diffusely distributed throughout both the fibrous cap and atheroma.
source: In the fibrous plaque, collagen VI is diffusely distributed throughout both the fibrous cap and atheroma (Katsuda et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Katsuda et al., 1992

claim: Treatment of ApoE-/- mice with antibodies to collagen VI reduces atherosclerosis.
source: Curiously, treatment of ApoE-/- mice with antibodies to collagen VI reduced atherosclerosis, but its exact role has remained unknown (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Liu et al., 2022

claim: Collagen VI is essential for early FA formation at the VSMC periphery and VSMC invasion in a 3D model.
source: Here, we showed that collagen VI is essential for early FA formation at the VSMC periphery as well as VSMC invasion in a 3D model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FA analysis and 3D invasion assays

claim: Collagen VI modulates FA formation either by activating cellular signalling or acting as a structural component changing local ECM stiffness.
source: We propose that collagen VI modulates FA formation either by activating cellular signalling or acting as a structural component changing local ECM stiffness (Sheetz et al., 1998).
evidence: Speculative proposal based on experimental observations and cited reference Sheetz et al., 1998

claim: Identified collagen VI receptors include α3β1 integrin, CSPG4 (NG2), and anthrax toxin receptors 1 and 2.
source: Identified collagen VI receptors include α3β1 integrin, the cell surface proteoglycan chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan-4 (CSPG4; also known as NG2), and the anthrax toxin receptors 1 and 2 (Doane et al., 1998; Nishiyama and Stallcup, 1993; Nanda et al., 2004; Burgi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by cited references Doane et al., 1998, Nishiyama and Stallcup, 1993, Nanda et al., 2004, and Burgi et al., 2017

claim: CMG2/ANTXR2 mediates localised Rho activation upon collagen VI binding.
source: Interestingly, a novel, recently identified Collagen VI signalling receptor (CMG2/ANTXR2) mediates localised Rho activation upon collagen VI binding (Burgi et al., 2017; Bürgi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by cited references Burgi et al., 2017 and Bürgi et al., 2020

claim: NG2 activates the Rho/ROCK pathway leading to effective amoeboid invasiveness of tumour cells characterised by excessive blebbing and enhanced actomyosin contractility.
source: NG2 also activates the Rho/ROCK pathway leading to effective amoeboid invasiveness of tumour cells which is characterised by excessive blebbing and enhanced actomyosin contractility (Sahai and Marshall, 2003; Paňková et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references Sahai and Marshall, 2003 and Paňková et al., 2012

claim: NG2 expression is elevated in VSMCs in atherosclerotic plaque.
source: Of note, it was also reported that NG2 expression is elevated in VSMCs in the atherosclerotic plaque and NG2 knockout prevents plaque formation (Tillet et al., 2002; She et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited references Tillet et al., 2002 and She et al., 2016

claim: NG2 knockout prevents plaque formation.
source: Of note, it was also reported that NG2 expression is elevated in VSMCs in the atherosclerotic plaque and NG2 knockout prevents plaque formation (Tillet et al., 2002; She et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited references Tillet et al., 2002 and She et al., 2016

claim: Endotrophin, a collagen VI α3 chain-derived profibrotic fragment, has been associated with higher risk of arterial stiffness and cardiovascular and all‐cause death in patients with type 1 diabetes and atherosclerosis.
source: Curiously, endotrophin, a collagen VI α3 chain-derived profibrotic fragment has recently been associated with a higher risk of arterial stiffness and cardiovascular and all‐cause death in patients with type 1 diabetes and atherosclerosis, respectively (Holm Nielsen et al., 2021; Frimodt-Møller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by cited references Holm Nielsen et al., 2021 and Frimodt-Møller et al., 2019

claim: The unique adhesion cluster in VSMC-derived sEVs includes EDIL3, TGFBI, and LGALS3BP, which are directly implicated in activation of integrin signalling and cellular invasiveness.
source: In addition to collagen VI, the unique adhesion cluster in VSMC-derived sEVS also includes EGF-like repeat and discoidin I-like domain-containing protein (EDIL3), transforming growth factor-beta-induced protein ig-h3 (TGFBI) and the lectin galactoside-binding soluble 3 binding protein (LGALS3BP), and these proteins are also directly implicated in activation of integrin signalling and cellular invasiveness (Lee et al., 2016; Costanza et al., 2019; Stampolidis et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited references Lee et al., 2016, Costanza et al., 2019, and Stampolidis et al., 2015

claim: FN stimulates sEV secretion by VSMCs.
source: We also identified a positive feedback loop and showed that FN stimulates sEV secretion by VSMCs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing FN effects on sEV secretion

claim: sEV secretion is governed by activation of G-protein-coupled receptors.
source: sEV secretion is a tightly regulated process which is governed by activation of signalling pathways including activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (Verweij et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by cited reference Verweij et al., 2018

claim: sEV secretion is governed by alterations in cytosolic calcium.
source: sEV secretion is a tightly regulated process which is governed by activation of signalling pathways including activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (Verweij et al., 2018) and alterations in cytosolic calcium (Savina et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by cited reference Savina et al., 2003

claim: sEV secretion is governed by small GTPases Rab7, Rab27a, Rab27b, and Rab35.
source: sEV secretion is a tightly regulated process which is governed by activation of signalling pathways including activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (Verweij et al., 2018) and alterations in cytosolic calcium (Savina et al., 2003), small GTPases Rab7, Rab27a, Rab27b, and Rab35 (Jaé et al., 2015; Savina et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by cited references Jaé et al., 2015 and Savina et al., 2002

claim: sEV secretion is governed by vesicular trafficking scaffold proteins including syntenin, sortillin, and CD63.
source: sEV secretion is a tightly regulated process which is governed by activation of signalling pathways including activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (Verweij et al., 2018) and alterations in cytosolic calcium (Savina et al., 2003), small GTPases Rab7, Rab27a, Rab27b, and Rab35 (Jaé et al., 2015; Savina et al., 2002), vesicular trafficking scaffold proteins including syntenin (Baietti et al., 2012), sortillin (Goettsch et al., 2016), and CD63 (van Niel et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by cited references Baietti et al., 2012, Goettsch et al., 2016, and van Niel et al., 2011

claim: sEV secretion is governed by accumulation of ceramide.
source: sEV secretion is a tightly regulated process which is governed by activation of signalling pathways including activation of G-protein-coupled receptors (Verweij et al., 2018) and alterations in cytosolic calcium (Savina et al., 2003), small GTPases Rab7, Rab27a, Rab27b, and Rab35 (Jaé et al., 2015; Savina et al., 2002), vesicular trafficking scaffold proteins including syntenin (Baietti et al., 2012), sortillin (Goettsch et al., 2016), and CD63 (van Niel et al., 2011) or accumulation of ceramide (Trajkovic et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Trajkovic et al., 2008

claim: Fibrillar ECM proteins FN and collagen I induce sEV secretion by activating the β1 integrin/FAK/Src and Arp2/3-dependent pathways.
source: We found that the fibrillar ECM proteins, FN and collagen I, induce sEV secretion by activating the β1 integrin/FAK/Src and Arp2/3-dependent pathways.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using inhibitors and activating/blocking antibodies

claim: In vivo FN staining data are in good agreement with previous studies showing accumulation of FN in late-stage plaques.
source: Our in vivo FN staining data are in good agreement with previous studies showing accumulation of FN in late-stage plaques (Langley et al., 2017; Glukhova et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by cited references Langley et al., 2017 and Glukhova et al., 1989

claim: Close co-distribution of FN and CD81 in the plaque suggests that accumulating FN matrices can stimulate sEV secretion in vivo.
source: Moreover, we observed close co-distribution of FN and CD81 in the plaque, suggesting that accumulating FN matrices can stimulate sEV secretion in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from colocalization data in plaques

claim: Expression of α5β1 integrin is re-activated upon VSMC de-differentiation following vascular injury.
source: Notably, expression of the major FN receptor, α5β1 integrin is re-activated upon VSMC de-differentiation following vascular injury (Pickering et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Pickering et al., 2000

claim: α5β1 integrin mediates FN matrix assembly, whilst β3 integrins are important for cell-matrix interactions.
source: It is thought the α5β1 integrin mediates FN matrix assembly, whilst β3 integrins are important for cell-matrix interactions (Pickering et al., 2000; Slepian et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by cited references Pickering et al., 2000 and Slepian et al., 1998

claim: α5β1 integrin functions as an ECM sensor inducing production of collagen VI-loaded sEVs which enhance cell invasion in the complex ECM meshwork.
source: Our data sheds new light on the functional role of α5β1 as an ECM sensor inducing production of collagen VI-loaded sEVs which in turn enhance cell invasion in the complex ECM meshwork.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results throughout the study

claim: Excessive collagen and elastin matrix breakdown in atheroma has been tightly linked to acute coronary events.
source: Excessive collagen and elastin matrix breakdown in atheroma has been tightly linked to acute coronary events; hence, it will be interesting to study the possible link between sEV secretion and plaque stability, as sEV-dependent invasion is also likely to influence the necessary ECM degradation induced by invading cells (Libby and Aikawa, 2002).
evidence: Supported by cited reference Libby and Aikawa, 2002

claim: Cooperative activation of integrin signalling and F-actin cytoskeleton pathways results in secretion of sEVs which associate with the ECM and play a signalling role by controlling FA formation and cell-ECM crosstalk.
source: In summary, cooperative activation of integrin signalling and F-actin cytoskeleton pathways results in the secretion of sEVs which associate with the ECM and play a signalling role by controlling FA formation and cell-ECM crosstalk (Figure 8).
evidence: Summary inference from all experimental results, illustrated in Figure 8
